size.note: Newman's Birds gives 14–15 cm. Wikipedia, citing HBW, gives 13 cm.

habitat: Rank vegetation along streams and gullies, reedbed and forest edges, and bracken or briar away from water. In the lowveld it is scarce.
summary: A bright yellow warbler of rank cover, with a browner crown and blackish legs. Males are bright yellow below with an olive wash on the sides. Females are duller yellow. Immatures are orange-yellow, with buffier wing edges, rump and tail. The colour of a newly hatched chick is not described in the texts used here. Older lists used the name Chloropeta natalensis.

similar.note: Icterine Warbler has bluish-grey legs, a pale wing panel and drier woodland. African Yellow Warbler has blackish legs and wetter, ranker cover.

bill.shape: slender; the upper mandible is pale and the lower mandible is blackish

underparts.pattern: bright yellow, with an olive wash on the sides of the breast, flanks and lower belly

viewNotes.note: Yellowish-brown upperparts, a yellower rump and brown flight feathers edged yellow. A separate upperwing pattern, such as a panel, is not described.
The underwing is not described in the texts used here.
A bright yellow throat and breast under a slightly browner crown. The bill is slender, pale above and blackish below.
Yellowish-brown upperparts and tail, with a yellower rump. The crown is a little browner than the back.
Yellow underparts, a dark cap, blackish legs and a longer tail than a yellow weaver. It usually stays low, then climbs a stem to sing.
Immatures are orange-yellow rather than bright yellow, and the wing edges, rump and tail are more buff.

calls.description: A quick, often-repeated trrp-trrp-chiri-chiri-chiri-chiri; the texts used here do not say that females sing a different song.
A sharp tsk or chirr; the texts used here do not assign the alarm to one sex.

research.note: Kemp classed it as a visiting breeder. SABAP1 found no seasonal movement in the atlas models and called it resident, with a post-breeding shift to lower altitudes in winter, and cited Tarboton and others for it being a rare visitor to the lowveld. Newman says it is present in lower-lying localities during winter. All twelve months are stored from that resident conclusion, not from a Kruger month count. The iris is not named in the texts used here. The underwing is not described. The alarm recording is grade B from Limpopo because no grade-A call was in the catalogue; the song is grade A from the Drakensberg. Chick down is not described. Wikipedia also gives the song as chip-chip-chip-whee-lee-wheeo; Newman’s transcription is the one stored because it is the southern African field guide.
